paras: The killing of Alfred Wiggins took place in Baltimore harbor early on May 12, 1881, when Policeman John B. Dorsey shot Wiggins, a Black man he suspected of stealing grain from the schooner Ida, and Wiggins fell overboard and drowned. A coroner's jury found the same day that Dorsey, on duty and in danger of his life, had been justified in using his pistol. Wire services carried it as a short crime item headed "A Dead Thief," and weekly digests repeated it the next week.

According to police testimony at the inquest, thefts of sacked grain from vessels anchored in the harbor had increased, and officers had been ordered to follow harbor thieves closely. Police Marshal Gray testified that Dorsey, a 13-year veteran and good rower, had been picked to watch for these "Hafenpiraten" (harbor pirates).

Wiggins, about 35, lived at 46 Mulberry Street, unloaded ships for a living, belonged to a Black Odd Fellows lodge, and left a wife and five children, according to Mary Pallner, a Black woman who identified him at the inquest. Policeman Peter Riley testified that he had arrested Wiggins in October 1880 with an anchor and old iron said to be stolen from a ship, a case sent to the grand jury without further result.

The only account of the encounter was Dorsey's own, given under oath at the inquest. He testified that at about 3 a.m., near West Falls Avenue, he saw a man in a small boat hiding by a wharf in the moonlight and then rowing toward the Ida, about 100 yards offshore. Dorsey borrowed a boat from the ferryman James Paul, followed, found the man's boat tied beside the schooner, and called out to him.

By Dorsey's account, the man answered with blows from a 12-foot oar to his head, arm and leg; Dorsey fired once and missed, fired again when struck at, and the man fell headfirst into the water. The wire version compressed this into a chase in which "the negro knocked him down with an oar" before Dorsey shot him in the thigh. Paul testified that he heard the blows and shots, and witnesses identified the boat Wiggins used as taken from Thomas Mitchell and the broken oar as Frank Dingle's. Men aboard the Ida could not recover him; the body was found after 6 a.m.

Coroner Walker held the inquest at the Middle District station house, where an autopsy found that the bullet had entered the left thigh without striking a main artery and that Wiggins had drowned. Marshal Gray told the jury that Wiggins would have killed Dorsey had he been able, and Captain Lannan called the officer cool-headed and reliable. The jury found that Dorsey, on duty and in danger, was justified in firing. Wire dispatches said only that "the Coroner exonerated Dorsey"; no report of further inquiry, charges or Black protest appears in the coverage.

The fullest report appeared on May 13 in Baltimore's German-language daily Der Deutsche Correspondent under the headline "Das Loos eines Hafenpiraten" (The fate of a harbor pirate). Built on the inquest testimony, it closed by describing Wiggins as nearly six feet tall and about 200 pounds, a man who would have been a very dangerous opponent in any struggle.

The same day an Associated Press dispatch ran in the Chicago Daily Tribune as "A Dead Thief" and in the Omaha Daily Bee as "A Negro Grain Thief Killed," both calling Wiggins "a negro harbor thief." The Memphis Daily Appeal gave two sentences to "Alfred Wiggins, colored" in a column headed "A Chapter of Horrors." Five days later a digest item about "a colored ship thief named Alfred Wiggan" ran in the Mower County Transcript, the Watertown Republican and the Superior Times.
Every account treated the theft as established and took the circumstances of the shooting from the police; none quoted Wiggins's family or associates.

Reports differ on the time: the wire said Wiggins was discovered "this forenoon" or "yesterday morning," the Memphis Appeal said "last night," and the digests said "the night of the 11th." The inquest report, based on sworn testimony, placed the shooting shortly before 3 a.m. on May 12 and is the most specific version.

reader.title: Killing of Alfred Wiggins
bases: A single on-duty policeman shot Wiggins while trying to stop a suspected harbor theft, and a coroner's jury ruled the shooting justified; no crowd or mob was involved (A3, A5).

The local German-language inquest report (A5), the Associated Press dispatch (A3, A4) and the separately worded Memphis item (A1) agree that Policeman Dorsey shot Wiggins in Baltimore harbor and that he drowned; all details of the encounter come from the officer's side.

accounts.label: Policeman Dorsey's sworn testimony
accounts.gist: He followed a man rowing toward the Ida, found his boat tied beside the schooner, called to him, and was struck repeatedly with a 12-foot oar; he fired once and missed, fired again when struck at, and the man fell headfirst into the water.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Wiggins drowned about 3 a.m. on May 12 after being shot in the thigh; Dorsey, on duty and in danger of his life, was justified in using his pistol.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A 'negro harbor-thief' stealing grain from the Ida was chased by Dorsey, knocked him down with an oar, was shot in the thigh, fell overboard and drowned; the coroner exonerated Dorsey.

framing.detail: The Baltimore German daily headlined 'Das Loos eines Hafenpiraten' (the fate of a harbor pirate), built the story on police testimony and closed by stressing Wiggins's size and strength as a 'very dangerous opponent'.
The AP dispatch ran as 'A DEAD THIEF' (Chicago) and 'A NEGRO GRAIN THIEF KILLED' (Omaha), calling Wiggins 'a negro harbor thief' and ending with the coroner's exoneration.
Memphis and Midwestern weeklies listed it as one item among unrelated killings in 'A Chapter of Horrors' and 'Tragical Tales'.

conflicts.note: The local inquest report rests on sworn testimony from the officer and the ferryman and is the most specific; the wire's 'forenoon' likely reflects when the body was found or the inquest held.
The inquest identification and the first-day reports give Wiggins.
